title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
book_title: Chapter 8: Reading the Tape and the Macro Regime

epigraph.quote: Even the strongest Stage 2 leader struggles to compound when the broader market logs ten distribution days and portfolio cash sits near three percent.
epigraph.author: Tape & Risk Desk

web_blocks.html: Technically, Eli Lilly remains in a confirmed Weinstein Stage 2 uptrend across both session snapshots, though short-term momentum has cooled from its $1,475.25 52-week high [35]. At the verified November 20, 2026 close of $1,347.11, LLY sits -8.69% below its 52-week peak, -2.66% below its 20-day SMA ($1,383.91), +6.33% above its rising 50-day SMA ($1,266.92), and +20.50% above its 200-day SMA ($1,117.90). Daily RSI(14) cooled to 49.50 with an ATR(14) of $42.43 (3.15% daily volatility).

The November 23 live TradingView and options snapshots show LLY rebounding +2.03% to $1,374.45 (options feed $1,373.57), lifting 1D RSI to 54.19 while 4H RSI sits at 46.25 and 1W RSI holds at 61.71 [35]. Bollinger bandwidth compressed to 13.24% above the rising 10-week EMA ($1,315.28) and 30-week SMA ($1,193.58), forming a textbook Stage 2 volatility contraction (VCP) inside the snapshot support zone of $1,295.55–$1,389.70 with an invalidation stop at $1,172.53 [35].

web_blocks.takeaway: While LLY retains a Stage 2 VCP structure on its chart, 6 stock distribution days, a 10-distribution-day market Downtrend, and 3.38% portfolio cash make chasing at $1,347–$1,374 poor risk management.

web_blocks.html: Crucially, tape structure cannot be separated from portfolio and macro context. On November 20, 2026, the U.S. market regime sits in a confirmed Downtrend: only 38.8% of tracked leaders trade above their 50-day SMA, only 1 of 11 sectors holds above its 20-day SMA, and the S&P 500 has logged 10 distribution days in the past 25 sessions. Simultaneously, our consolidated U.S. portfolio holds just $2,540.35 in cash (3.38% of $75,110.60 NAV) against a 22.0% Downtrend cash floor.

We also evaluate the automated options package: a February 19, 2027 (88 DTE) $1,360/$1,640 Bull Call Debit Spread priced at $93.17 net debit ($9,317.00 max loss) with a $1,453.17 breakeven (+5.8%) and 42.6% ATM IV vs. 35.9% HV20. Despite a theoretical 2.01:1 max payoff if LLY clears $1,640, we decline this trade. One contract risks 12.40% of total portfolio NAV (3.67x our entire cash balance) and loses 100% of premium if LLY simply stalls below $1,360—or even rises to our $1,450.00 Base Fair Value, which sits below the $1,453.17 breakeven.

book_paragraphs: On a pure price chart, Eli Lilly still looks like a market general taking a breather. At the November 20, 2026 close of $1,347.11, the stock sits comfortably above its rising 50-day moving average at $1,266.92 and well clear of its 200-day moving average at $1,117.90. By November 23, live TradingView quotes showed a 2 percent rebound to $1,374.45, keeping the stock inside a tight 13.24 percent Bollinger bandwidth contraction.

Yet two warning lights flash beneath that Stage 2 surface. First, Lilly itself has logged six distribution days over the past 25 sessions, and its four-hour RSI remains below 50 at 46.25, showing that buyers have not yet reclaimed short-term control below the 20-day moving average at $1,383.91. Second, the broader U.S. market is in a confirmed Downtrend with ten distribution days and only 38.8 percent of stocks above their 50-day averages.

In a ten-distribution-day Downtrend, even Stage 2 leaders routinely break support or chop sideways for months while valuation multiples compress. That risk is magnified by our own portfolio posture: with $2,540.35 in cash—just 3.38 percent of our $75,110.60 net worth—against a 22 percent Downtrend cash floor, every dollar of scarce liquidity carries a steep opportunity cost.

book_subsections.title: Why We Decline the $1,360/$1,640 Bull Call Spread
paragraphs: The automated options desk surfaced an 88-day $1,360/$1,640 bull call debit spread expiring February 19, 2027 for $93.17 per share, or $9,317 per contract. On paper, a $9,317 risk for $18,683 of maximum profit looks like a clean 2.01-to-1 setup.

In practice, three flaws rule it out. First, a $9,317 debit consumes 12.40 percent of total portfolio equity and exceeds our entire $2,540 cash reserve by more than threefold. Second, implied volatility at 42.6 percent sits well above 20-day realized volatility at 35.9 percent, meaning you are overpaying for time value. Third, the spread's $1,453.17 expiration breakeven sits above our $1,450.00 base fair value, leaving negative expected value in a Downtrend tape.

callouts.title: Options Sizing & Breakeven Rejection
callouts.text: Risking $9,317 (12.4% of NAV) on an elevated-IV call spread that needs LLY above $1,453.17 by February 2027 violates both portfolio risk limits and our $1,450.00 fundamental fair value.
